newsitem.title: USA: Seagram's chief Bronfman wants Time Warner to lower debt.
newsitem.headline: Seagram's chief Bronfman wants Time Warner to lower debt.

text.p: Seagram Co. Chairman Edgar Bronfman Sr., the third-biggest stockholder in Time Warner Inc., says he wants to see the media giant reduce its $18 billion debt as a way to increase the value of its stock.

In an interview with Reuters Television Tuesday night, Bronfman declined to comment on what he thought of Time Warner Chairman Gerald Levin's handling of the company, but said, "We obviously are disappointed that the stock has not moved the way we think it should have moved."
He added, "I personally think they have too many assets tied up in what I call hardware -- cable and other things and not enough in content, (although) they are very big in content."

Bronfman owns 9.8 percent of Time Warner, while Ted Turner owns 11 percent of the media giant's stock and Liberty Media has a 10 percent non-voting share. A Time Warner spokesman said the company's debt was $18 billion.

Bronfman said he thought the company's real problem is "that they have just too much debt. They can't seem to come up from under the debt. I wish they would come up with a plan, which I think they are trying very hard to do.
"They are trying to make sense out of their balance sheet and when they do this, their stock will appreciate and we will be a happy investor," the 67-year-old Bronfman said.
Time Warner's stock was up 12.5 cents at $44.125 Wednesday on the New York Stock Exchange, near its 12-month high. For the year, it has fallen as low as $29.75.
In the interview, Bronfman also indicated that criticism of Seagrams' Universal Music Group distribution of rap records with controversial lyrics had struck home.

Bronfman's son Edgar Jr., who is chief executive officer of Seagram and its MCA division, was roundly attacked last year by critics of the company's distributing so-called "gangsta rap" with objectionable sexual lyrics.
Asked about the criticsm, Bronfman Sr. said, "Rap music is controversial, but it is what the street wants today. We have been careful about what we issue and don't issue.

"Perhaps we have leaned a little bit too far into agreeing to some things that are not acceptable. But we will learn. Our intentions are that we should not be producing anything that most people find objectionable."
